questions.q: What are the four layers of the TCP/IP model, bottom to top?
questions.explain: TCP/IP's four layers, bottom to top, are Network Access, Internet, Transport, and Application.

questions.q: Which TCP/IP layer absorbs OSI's Application, Presentation, and Session layers?
questions.explain: TCP/IP's single Application layer covers what OSI splits into three layers — real protocols like HTTP handle format and session concerns themselves.

questions.q: A firewall rule is described as operating "at Layer 4." What is it actually filtering on?
questions.explain: Layer 4 is the Transport layer in both models — filtering here means filtering based on TCP or UDP port numbers.

questions.q: As data moves down the stack from an application toward the wire, what does each layer do to the data from the layer above it?
options: Wraps it in its own header — encapsulation
Converts it directly to radio waves
questions.explain: Each layer encapsulates the data above it in its own header — a TCP segment wraps application data, an IP packet wraps the TCP segment, and an Ethernet frame wraps the IP packet.

questions.q: Why does TCP/IP, not OSI, matter more for understanding what a packet capture tool like Wireshark actually shows you?
options: Wireshark only works with OSI, not TCP/IP
Because TCP/IP is the model real networks actually implement, so Wireshark's nested headers (Ethernet, IP, TCP) reflect TCP/IP's real encapsulation
Wireshark doesn't show headers at all
OSI and TCP/IP produce completely different packets on the wire
questions.explain: TCP/IP is what's actually implemented on the wire, so the nested headers Wireshark displays (Ethernet frame containing an IP packet containing a TCP segment) directly reflect TCP/IP's real encapsulation process.
